utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before you close the blinds -- good morning to all. Before I call for the appearances, it would have been obvious to everyone over the past few days that Judge Harhoff has been struggling with the after effects of the flu, and this morning this got the better of him and he is not with us so, therefore, we are reconvened under the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Before we go into closed session to make certain inquiries, I would ask for the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan, who will be entering the court any minute now, appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we should -- yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was just going to say, Your Honour, if we could go into closed session to deal with protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, to begin with, can I ask you to have a look, please, at a sheet of paper and confirm that your name is shown on it with pseudonym ST-172?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that then be produced as an Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Exhibit P471 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, can we briefly go into private session while I deal with the witness's background.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may, Ms. Korner, now that we are back in open session, something that I neglected to do earlier, and that is to explain to the witness that you will be referred to as Witness or by number 172. The other thing I should point out to you not having given evidence before the Tribunal previously, the procedure is that you will be asked questions by the side that's calling you, in this case the Prosecution, then you will be -- there will be an opportunity for cross-examination by counsel for each of the accused, then re-examination by the Prosecution and the Chamber may have questions of you. It is anticipated that your testimony will extend into tomorrow. Yes. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just on that matter, in fact, I think you've already had an opportunity to meet Mr. Krgovic, counsel for Mr. Zupljanin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I want to ask you, please, a little bit about Manjaca camp itself. I think it was originally established in 1991 to hold prisoners of war from the Croatian conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I want to ask you now, please, a little bit about the layout of the camp and show you a short clip from a video as well. Can you first of all, please have a look at what has been marked, I hope, 3440.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I explain, this document, it will come in formally through another witness. It's part of a package for another witness. So it's not on our 65 ter list because it's part of the general package, but that's when it will be formally exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, is it on your list of documents for use?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, if you look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there's an English translation of the writing below. Is it possible to have the two side by side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir -- thank you very much. You had an opportunity to look at this diagram I think a couple of days ago. Do you agree that it's a pretty accurate depiction of what the camp was like when you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what has been marked on it, we can see, I don't think we need to go through it, what the various buildings were, and also where the guards were stationed. Does the dotted, the sort of barbed wire line, does that mark the perimeter of the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, the outside perimeter of the camp which is the area where the prisoners were housed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you now look, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This one was added in, Your Honours, I think the day before yesterday. 10234. Your Honour, I suppose that diagram ought to be marked for identification. As I say, it will come in as part of a 65 ter package -- 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P472 marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now can we have up -- what did I say? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, this is a document that you had a chance to see yesterday or the day before yesterday. These photographs, can I just say, were taken in 2001, but as far as you are concerned, are those photographs that were taken some nine years later pretty much depict what it was like in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, marked on this map, first of all, is Kljuc, which we can see to the left of where Manjaca was. Can you tell us, sir, roughly the distance between Kljuc, the town of Kljuc and Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Around 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whilst we are on that, were you ever aware of an incident where prisoners being brought to Manjaca had to walk from Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: I was aware of that, but I didn't see it myself, because I was absent that day or those few days from Manjaca, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, can we have that redacted please, on the public session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, can I just remind you that when we are in open session, if you could avoid explaining who was whom. Can you tell us what time of year, it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what, can you remember, I know it's a long time ago now, but can you remember what the weather was like that summer, in July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Generally speaking that summer was rather to the advantage of the prisoners. It was hot and there was no snow until the closure of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who brought the prisoners there who had to walk?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't mean a name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: -- they were brought by police officers from Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what, as you understand it, was the explanation for why these prisoners were made to walk from Kljuc to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: From what I know and the explanations that I had, there were no vehicles available and the distance was not too great, and that's how they decided to walk them from Kljuc. There were no motor vehicles to transfer them, that's the explanation I got.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And second question before we put this map away is, Manjaca to Banja Luka, how long -- what was the distance there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Maybe I'll say something different to what I said before, but it's around 35 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Your Honours, may that be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P473, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, can I ask you to look, please, at a short clip of a video that was also made in 2001, because that puts it really into perspective, the various pictures. We may stop it every now and again so that you can just tell us what we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What do we see here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's a building within the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: It was a workshop of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again can we pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Those are the offices and an area where the -- where the military police was housed and the camp commander as well. So they were offices basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause it -- while we are still paused, who was the camp commander when you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Bozidar Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine. Let's carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Those were workshops again which used to belong to that farm, and they had an infirmary there too where the prisoners were examined in one of those facilities. I think it was the last door actually in the row, so it was an infirmary. And a warehouse too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I suppose we should say that originally Manjaca was a farm, still is a farm; is that right? You have to say yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was a farm called Karadjordjevo they had sheep, they did sheep farming, livestock, cows, and even horses, and there were potatoes were grown, wheat corn, well, not wheat, it's too high up for that but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, can we -- yes, can we just move on on the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that one of the watchtowers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is the only watchtower, I think, that existed. We built it when the camp came into existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think this is fairly obvious because we've seen the photographs, is this one of the sheds in which prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's right. That is one of the sheds, and when the farm was in existence, cattle were kept there, but since they were left empty and there was the need to accommodate the detainees, then that's where they were accommodated. We called them pavilions. The prisoners were in six rows, so looking at the screen to the right, two rows of prisoners were there, and then there was this high -- platform higher up, two rows there and two rows to the left. And each pavilion could take 6- to 700 prisoners and there were six of those pavilions housing the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. All right, if we move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see there some sort of open structure, as it were. What was that used for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, this open structure, I think there were two of them, and that's where the prisoners had their meals. The food was cooked there, and they had their meals there under that shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Move on again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What are we -- can we just pause again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What are we going into here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, we are going to have to redact what he said about what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, there, can you just very briefly explain, it's obviously a church, but what significance it has?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: This is a church in the village of Sljivno, and it's at a distance of 2 kilometres away from where the prisoners were. The church had been destroyed quite a lot and the walls, the outer walls were left standing, and with respect to the people in the camp and some plans to complete the church, the corps commander ordered that the prisoners be involved in some of the construction work on the church. And so masons were found and so on and we saw to the windows and covered the church so it was reconstructed in 1992 while the prisoners were there by the prisoners or in part by the prisoners. It was repaired by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. That's all we need to ask. Your Honours, may I ask that that video clip -- video be admitted as -- it's on our 65 ter list, 2314.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interruption, can we have the date when this video was taken?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can probably find out, but I think it's June 2001 -- it's 2001 definitely, we'll give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, may I ask two just small questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you said the camp was set up as a prisoners of war camp from prisoners of war from Croatia. Mr. Popovic, was he the camp commander right from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. As to that time when the prisoners from Croatia were at Manjaca, I know nothing about that, nor was I physically there at that time. I just know the origins of the camp, how the camp came into being in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Popovic, what was his -- where did he come from? Was he someone from the military, or was he camp commander from his previous profession as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Popovic was an officer of the JNA, and then the Army of Republika Srpska and as such he was appointed camp commander sometime around the 15th of June 1992, so a little before I arrived or when I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's right, isn't it, that in fact he was a retired officer who had been brought back? Do you know that? If not, say so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I think he had retired but he was re-activated because of the war, like many others. Because a military conscript does not cease to be a conscript when he retires. I mean, their responsibility doesn't cease, but it ceases when they reach a certain age.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine. Now, I want to deal just briefly with who was guarding the prisoners in the camp. Were the majority of the guards drawn from the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But was there also involvement by civilian police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right, but for a limited time. Sometime in June when the need arose because there was a shortage of personnel in the military police, then through the corps command an order was given that the public security stations of Kljuc, Sanski Most, and I don't know which other police stations should make up a schedule and send part of their forces, 20 to 30 policemen in actual fact, as reinforcement for the external security of the camp, the perimeter of the camp. So that was done in July/August at the outset, as the last date, July and August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The civilian police, you say, were reinforcement for the external security of the camp, the perimeter. Was there anything in the regulations about whether they could enter the camp itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: There was an internal regulation issued by the camp commander which stated that the civilian police providing external security cannot enter the camp, not even the military police could enter the camp itself, unless there was a need for some kind of intervention, so only some forces were able to enter the camp without weapons. That is to say, within the wire fence that we were looking at earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And which were the forces that were allowed to come within the perimeter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: The military police commander would set up a schedule, a duty roster, for his men for special interventions or whatever they were called, I can't remember quite now, but anyway, there was a -- the intervention patrol was the only one allowed to enter the camp if some situation had to be resolved or if there was some threat or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The civilian police that were there, were they ever used to do duty in the observation tower?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, those are what the regulations said. Are you able to say one way or another whether military police and/or civilian -- it's two questions -- first of all, whether military police entered into the perimeter of the camp when they were not supposed to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I don't think I can answer that because I actually don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about civilian police, are you able to say one way or another whether, in breach of regulations, they entered within the perimeter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: According to my information that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whilst we are dealing with the civilian police, whilst they were on duty at the camp, whether from Kljuc or Sanski Most or wherever, under whose authority would they come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that on the basis of a corps command order and the public security centre, there was an agreement made, I don't know when and where but it was at that level generally, the corps commander and the public security centre on that level, it was decided that the public security stations or police stations of Kljuc, Sanski Most, should send a number of men according to their schedule and roster, and they would come in and that was resubordination on the basis of resubordination. As soon as they arrived at Manjaca, they were under the corps command or camp command, or rather the army. They were resubordinated to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if, for example, a civilian police officer committed, first of all, a disciplinary offence, who would deal with it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: The camp commander mostly, since it was a disciplinary offence, and he might inform the chief of the public security station as his -- the man superior that that happened. But generally in the camp because he was resubordinated to the camp command, so everything that happened within the camp came under the camp commander's responsibility, and he dealt with any issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If the civilian police officer committed an actual crime, in other words, for example, assaulted a prisoner, would it still be the camp commander who dealt with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Well, you would have to look at the nature of the crime committed, whether it was a crime or an infraction or what, but if it came under the responsibility of the camp commander, then he would deal with it. But if it was a crime and there was -- and serious bodily harm was caused as a result of the assault, then that would be up to the military court and military court judge, an investigation would be conducted, as was the case in the actual matter we are going to deal with in due course, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, are you referring to the Filipovic and Bender killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it was a crime and the military court judge would be brought in, would the facts be made known to the chief of the whichever SJB the officer came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Certainly, and that is logical. His superior would be informed about what had happened and the military court would take it further and initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, are you personally aware of any instances, leaving aside the Filipovic/Bender killings, where a civilian police officer was disciplined by the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know of any such case. I'm not aware of a case like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know, as we started late, are we going -- we are going on, are we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's, as you know, I follow the clock in LiveNote. It's 10.19 but I do intend to stick with the schedule so working backward from the time at which we must rise at 1.45, so we'll break at 10.25.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, can we go into private session for the next few minutes while I just deal with some other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you now, please, when a -- when prisoners arrived at the camp by and large who brought them to the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: For the most part in the greatest number of cases they were brought by members of the Ministry of the Interior, the police or milicija as we called them then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when the prisoners in -- were brought into the camp, who would deal with them first of all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: As they came into the camp itself, is that what you are asking?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, when they were brought in, what procedure was followed in respect of the prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: All right, I understand. You are asking me about the procedure of admittance. Once the prisoners were brought, we had already developed a certain procedure of admittance, and they would be first received by a commission. On that commission there were two policemen, one doctor, one person keeping records, and one representative of the security organ, (redacted). That was the commission receiving prisoners upon their arrival. We thought it most appropriate to take people in in groups of ten, and that was suitable to the size of the room. They would lean against the wall. They would be inspected by a policeman, stripped, checked by a doctor for any visible injuries. The secretary would take down the name of the prisoner either from his own words or from the documents he had on him, and all this was monitored by one of my men. The secretary would write the information in the book of records of prisoners and in the medical record. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just please redact the words at line 18 before it goes out to the public, "(redacted)" Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can I ask you now about the doctor that you've mentioned. Would that be a doctor, a military doctor or someone who was a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: The doctors were from the ranks of prisoners, Eniz Sabanovic and Derviskadic, Mehmed Derviskadic. They were also prisoners but they were professional doctors and they were very good at their work and very disciplined, and on behalf of our medical service, there was a nurse, Aleksandar Bijelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The paperwork you told us that was sometimes not available, were there any times when prisoners were admitted without any kind of paper, in other words, an identification card or anything at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the status of these prisoners? In other words, what -- this was a military camp, what were these prisoners supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: We did not make any distinction in that respect. It was all the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But we'll see in various documents they are described as POWs or prisoners of war. What was your understanding of what a prisoner of war was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: I can only give you the textbook definition. A person of the opposite warring party trained, uniformed, captured on the frontline. That's what I understand to be a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think this is right, isn't it, that you had training in the conventions which govern the treatment of such prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move, please, first of all to the documents. Can you have a look, please, first of all at P60.12.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'd like to go, please, in the English to the third page and in the B/C/S to the fourth page, I believe. No, it's typed, in the B/C/S, please, it's maybe the fifth. That's it, right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a list which I don't believe, sir, you saw -- you'd seen before you looked at it here because it comes from the Sanski Most police station, but it's headed "List of the Most Radical Extremists in the Area of Sanski Most." And the person shown at number 4 is a gentleman by the same of Eniz Sabanovic. Is that the doctor you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: I think so. The first and last names are the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Presumably over the period that he was in the camp you had a number of dealings with him, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there anything about his conversations or anything about what you learned about him to suggest that he was, as described, the most radical -- one of the most radical extremists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Not that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next could you have a look, please, at document P61.2. Sir, this is -- at the top I think it's got written "assistant commander for moral guidance. Deliver to the warden of the Manjaca camp, personally inspect how prisoners of war are being treated." It's actually a document that was signed by Mladic and deals with what is called "Accommodation for the Prisoners of War and the Principles." It's dated the 15th of June, which is the day you arrived, but were you made aware of the contents of this order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: No, I had not seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I appreciate you weren't shown the document, but were you made aware that General Mladic had issued this instruction about the treatment of the prisoners of Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, it was done several times both by the corps command and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next could we have a look, please, at document 65 ter 456. Sorry, we need to go in the English to the second page and in the B/C/S to the third page, I think it is. It should be paragraph 5 in each case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, sir, I don't think you ever saw this document because it's a report to the 1st Krajina -- by the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff. But paragraph 5 dealing with security situations says: "About 900 prisoners of war from Stari Gradiska have been moved to Manjaca." First, were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: When I arrived at Manjaca, those people were already there and from the course of events I knew they had been brought from Stari Gradiska because that place was in the Republic of Croatia, and according to the Vance Owen Plan all members of the army and the army in general had to leave Croatia and move, and since the prisoners had been in the Stari Gradiska prison, they were relegated following orders from the corps command to another sector, that is Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just tell us, who were the prisoners? What nationality were the prisoners from Stari Gradiska, by and large?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: The prisoners were mostly of Muslim ethnicity, there were a few Croats, and perhaps a few Serbs were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the Serbs who were there, what had they been in prison for in Stari Gradiska? What sort of crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: I'm not trying to say that there were Serbs from Stari Gradiska, but at Manjaca in general when I was trying to produce some sort of statistics, I found there were five Serbs. I remember specifically one man named Medic who was captured as a member of the Croatian units in Slavonia. He had been mobilised in Zagreb, and he was a member of the Croatian Armed Forces, and he was captured in Slavonia and ended up in Stari Gradiska and then Manjaca. And there may have been a few other Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you just give us roughly, you say mostly the prisoners were of Muslim ethnicity, were you able to ascertain from the paperwork that came with them, what crimes they were alleged to have committed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Are you asking about only those from Stari Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking about Stari Gradiska, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, in Stari Gradiska, the camp or the prison, there was a large group of Muslims from the Grapska village, around 300 of them, and they arrived at Manjaca. The charges were the same, the circumstances were the same as with other prisoners. They had been found carrying weapons or on the front line. The charges were similar to those against other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document is on our 65 ter list, I wonder if that could be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P475, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next could we have a look at 65 ter 2855.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document originating from Kljuc SJB, and it's a list of those who were members of the Territorial Defence, and what I want to ask you about is firstly this: Vinko Kondic, a chief of Kljuc, SJB signed this, did you see him ever at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did he come to the camp for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: At the invitation of Colonel Stevilovic. They had a problem to solve and I saw the two of them together, and I was present during their conversation. That's when I met the man and never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to spend too much time on what the problem was, but what did it concern, the problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: It was precisely about the documentation. They tried to reach an agreement, that is Stevilovic told Kondic not to send any more people without documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the handwritten part of the document shows that detainees were admitted by Sergeant Milorad Topic. Who was Sergeant Milorad Topic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: He was some sort of secretary keeping records at the camp, part of the military police, and I think he is mentioned in connection with the Filipovic murder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to Sergeant Milorad Topic in respect to the Filipovic murder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: The same as others who were involved. They were suspended immediately, dismissed from their duty, an on-site investigation team headed by an investigating judge was invited to conduct an autopsy with the help of a doctor, and they were sent away and turned over to the jurisdiction of the competent court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when were these member -- these people tried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Those people were tried, the killers of Filipovic and Bender, in 2007, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we redact those last words, please. Your Honours, may that document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P476, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, the next document is one of the witness's documents. Can it not, therefore, go up on the screen. Yes, can you -- could we have up on the screen for us though, not the screen for the public, please, document number 2462.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, is this one of the reports that you were talking about that you sent to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we can see your initials at the second page, but we needn't bother with that for the moment. It begins, dated the 22nd of June and begins: "During the day we processed a group of prisoners older than 60 and a group younger than 18 in order to release these individuals..." What was the relevance of the over 60 and under 18?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Well, we followed on from some sort of logic of military responsibility and duty, and a person from 18 to 60 by law, the law of the day, was considered to have a military duty. And if there was no other incrimination to the effect that that person had committed some offence or crime or war crime because anybody can commit a war crime of course, but if that wasn't there then we considered that those people should be released from the camp or that we should take steps to have them released.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then can we go to the third paragraph, please, where you talk about an interview that was conducted with Mr. Hadzic, and the report says: "It has been established that he came to Manjaca by mistake." What did you words "by mistake" mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: It means that the organ that brought him in provided us with information which said that he was -- that he had actually been taken to Manjaca by mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They told you that, the people who brought him in? The police officers who brought him in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Either the police officers who brought him in, but I doubt that this was uncovered straightaway, but some document must have arrived subsequently from the police station, or there might have been some intervention on somebody's part to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the rest of the document talks about your interview with the late Filipovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, may that be marked and admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P477 under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next could you have a look, please, at the document which is at -- yes, 65 ter 810.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document emanating from Vinko Kondic again to the command of the prisoner of war camp as agreed between Colonel Stevilovic and the chief of the Kljuc SJB, inspectors Todo Gajic and Dmitar Buvac are sent to process the prisoners of war. Was this as a result of the discussion which Colonel Stevilovic had with Inspector Kondic? You have to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you meet inspector Gajic and the other gentleman at all while they were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you've told us, when they question prisoners, there wouldn't have been any member present of the intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, may that be marked -- admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P478, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next document is 65 ter 10224, and I tell Your Honours straightaway, for some reason this did not materialise on to our 65 ter list, but it's another report from this witness and, therefore, I'd ask it not be put up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's dated the 26th of June, sir, and is that right, it's one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What you are dealing with for a large part, is this right, is in paragraph 3, the fact that there are sources amongst the prisoners, people who are providing information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then in the fourth paragraph, 46 prisoners have been received from Bosanska Dubica, and it appears they've been processed already by the SJB, and it says they were brought to Manjaca camp only for accommodation and guarding purposes. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That means that they would be there until they could be put up by the investigating centre of the military court in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why would they be kept in Manjaca which is a military prisoner of war camp rather than in Bosanska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: I think, I can only say what I think and make logical conclusions while they were there, I suppose, because of the space available or not. But I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then over on the second page of the English, I think it's all on one page on the B/C/S, there are by June already -- 26th of June, 1.548 prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, now, Your Honours, I know that the rule is it's not on our 65 ter, can't have it admitted. But, Your Honour, this is so obviously a relevant document, and I'm afraid when one is going through it, these slip through the net sometimes, so I'm asking to have it admitted and exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Any observations by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P479, under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then could we have 65 ter 2427. Again if we can not have that put on the public screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Another report, in fact the following day, with your initials, which talks about 39 new prisoners from Sanski Most. Sanski Most inspectors are going to come back to continue the processing. 103 from Kljuc, two people from Sanski Most who have helped out are going to be released, and now the next day we jump from -- because of the new prisoners from 1.568 to 1.700 prisoners; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I don't want to spend any more time on that. Could that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P480, perhaps under seal, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all these documents under seal, please. I'm sorry, I should make that clear.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next document, please, number 10225. Your Honours, not on our 65 ter but it's going to come in as part of a 92 ter package so this can just be marked for identification. Could we go to the second page in each case, I think it is. And can we just for a moment go into private session, please. Just for one question.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That will be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P482 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Another report dated the 1st of July, and in the middle, can we go down the page a bit. The words: "According to the updated records, there is 1.000 -- over -- well, nearly, in fact, 1.100 prisoners from Kljuc. 229 from Doboj, 268 from Sanski Most, 34 from Prijedor" and so on and so forth. And then more than 95 per cent of these prisoners are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go over the page in English, but I believe it's all one page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The report says: "We are suggesting considering releasing all prisoners older than 60 and all minors up to 18 years of age, as well as seriously sick people, if they did not commit war crimes." Now that's the second time we've had this reference to releasing. The first report was about a fortnight before that. Had anything been done about the suggestion that the over 60 and under 18 should be released? In other words, had anything happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Since the previous report to this one, of course nothing happened. We did make the proposals, and we'll be coming across later reports where this is touched upon as a problem and dealt with in the reports, but I thought that it might not be that easy to accomplish with the chain of command and so on while it goes to the powers that be and is sent back, so I wasn't expecting an immediate reaction anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you thought it was worth repeating the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly that's what I considered. And I did repeat it, and you will find it five or six times. The problem was raised again five or six times subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could we now, please, have a look at the document which is 10227. It's not on our 65 ter list and only I'm going to ask that it's marked for identification at the moment. But again I'm going to ask -- sorry, we better do this in private session. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's one of your reports, sir, 4th of July, and by then the prisoner count has risen to 1.870 people. That's in the paragraph there. And again, sir, as you say, the suggestion is being made that the over 60s and the younger than 18 should be released, so nothing happened by the 4th of July either; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's right, yes. Nothing happened. None of the measures proposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P484 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 2468, please, next document. Same thing, under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. This is the 5th of July. You are dealing with the 268 prisoners of war from Sanski Most, and you say that sufficient paperwork to submit criminal reports against the individual who merit to have criminal reports which will be done by the authorised officials from the SJB Sanski Most. So was it the job of the authorised officials', as they are described, from the SJBs responsibility to file criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's right, that was their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And yet again you say that the Sanski Most SJB being given the individuals older than 60 and younger than 18 in order to discuss the possibility of their returning to their place of residence, and the sick. So again you are repeating what you said, as we can see, over and over again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please. That was on our 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it on your --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't see it on your list of documents for use with 172?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the top of the second page, 2468.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm not in pages. 468, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 2468, okay. On the record is 468.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't catch that. It's 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P485 [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next can we move to 65 ter 1592 again please under seal and not to be put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, for the record, the previous one, I suppose it's under seal as well, but it's not mentioned in the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, that will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is your report three days after the last and you say this in the middle of the first paragraph: "It is characteristic, as was the case with previously processed prisoners, that a large majority of prisoners brought to Manjaca POW camp had no weapons, nor were they actively participated in the organisation of the implementation of the armed rebellion. This makes it -- this fact makes it difficult to collect and compile documentation on criminal acts necessary for the functioning of illegal activities." That's what you wrote, sir. Was that your opinion in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's correct. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then you go on to deal with this incident: "In the course of 7th July 1992, 560 prisoners from Sanski Most were admitted to Manjaca camp. During transport from Sanski Most to Manjaca, 24 prisoners died. The most probable cause was lack of oxygen as they were transported in refrigerator trucks. Such conduct on the part of the organs from Sanski Most is extremely inhumane and unprofessional. The people who died were not admitted, and they are not considered to have been POWs in Manjaca. The mistakes that were noticed earlier, such as bringing in people younger than 18 and older than 60, still continue." Now, were you present the day before you wrote this when these prisoners arrived with these dead people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was there when they were brought? Who had brought them in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Police officers from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was their attitude, if you can recall, as to the fact that 24 people had died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall individual reactions, but I personally was astounded because among the people who were standing up like -- packed like sardines. It was not in fact a refrigerator truck, it was a truck covered with tarpaulin, but the trailer part is connected to the camp, and some people were already old and infirm or had health problems and that contributed to their death. But in any case, 24 persons were taken out of the truck dead and they could not be re-animated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You refused, not surprisingly, one can say, to take in the dead bodies. Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: We admitted only living people, so the bodies were returned, although I have no proof of it, by the same trailer truck to Sanski Most, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then finally on this document, you talk about the death of someone from Kljuc who died of natural causes and that Manjaca camp was visited by presidents of the municipal district and military courts in Banja Luka. I think that's all we need on that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that please be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P486 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we look, please, at the next document which is 2428 on our 65 ter. Again it's a report, so I'd ask that it be admitted and marked under seal. And not shown on the public screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You again talk about the problems relating to these prisoners "relating to the reception of the new prisoners, especially from the municipalities Kljuc and Sanski Most, as they are being brought in massively, in large quantities no selection is being made. They are bringing those who shouldn't be treated as prisoner of war because they are being picked up from their homes and off their fields. Individuals older than 60, younger than 18, no attention is being paid to transportation, and the prisoners, (who are humans after all) are dying of thirst and lack of oxygen. Prisoners also during the transportation are not being treated in line with the Geneva Conventions, they are maltreated, beaten, and humiliated in the extreme." When you wrote that, sir, was that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: I didn't see the signature below, but I believe it's my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom of the page just to confirm the initials. It's second page in B/C/S, sorry, and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's it. Yes, it's my report. Yes, that's what I wrote. I have no proof for what I wrote and no way to clarify or explain further, but sometimes I reacted like this to express my own feelings and to force those to whom the report was addressed to react in some way, to put a stop to do these things, bringing in people en masse who did not deserve to be brought in, and that's the feeling I had from the statements of those people who were brought in, which again does not necessarily mean that they were so truthful with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, exactly, of course, you couldn't know they were truthful, but do we gather from this that there was a theme with all the questioning that was being carried out that these people had not been fighting or armed or in uniform but had simply been taken off the fields, as you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, one could conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you felt it necessary to stress that prisoners were also human beings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Precisely. I always believed that as long as I was in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P487, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just look, please, at the document which is 65 ter 1113. And can we look at paragraph 4 in the English and in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is not a document that I think you saw before. It's a combat report but we can see -- without going into further details -- it should not be -- sorry, it shouldn't be on the screen. Well, it doesn't matter. Sorry, I take that back. The gentleman who has signed that report is the gentleman about whom you've been talking; is that right? Can you just say yes or no to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look at -- sorry, if we look at the bottom of probably is the second page in -- it's the second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back to paragraph 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It says: "105 Muslim prisoners were today handed over to the Merhamet organisation. These were the prisoners who had not been charged with any crimes." Then it goes on about the Muslim and Croats who want to leave. Was that the first release of any prisoners whilst you had been there? Well, firstly, I should ask you, is that right? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. And I believe it was the first time, thanks to the activity of the Merhamet charity because all these other things, the bringing of older and to young people, all these complaints, nobody paid any attention, so Merhamet took over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm not sure whether the Trial Chamber has heard about Merhamet before? You have. Yes. Thank you very much. Could that be marked, please -- admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P488, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And just before the break, because I think this is connected with the same thing, can you look, please, at document 2429.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We haven't typed out all the names, but is this some of the people who were released into Merhamet as approved by Colonel Vukelic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes. These are people younger than 18, or 18 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, again it's on our 65 ter, admitted and marked. This one need not be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P489, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's time for the break or not, Your Honours, I'm seeing there's one short document I can do before the break. No, the next document, Your Honour, is a long one and deals with Filipovic, so that may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as the witness is being escorted back to the stand, I would alert you that you have 30 minutes of your allotted time left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I rather thought that I had asked for three hours but [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mrs. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I will see if I can ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say, I can do this if I simply ask for admittance of documents on our 65 ter list which I don't have time to deal with but which are on our list for this witness, so that I don't go through all of them with him, but they are admitted. It's going through the documents that takes the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If that is the most efficient way that you have of dealing with it, because time of course, remains crucial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I think Your Honours must be seeing why I'm taking a little bit of time with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, Your Honours, I'll do my level best and see where we get to in the next half-hour. Can I ask, sir, that the next document that we have up on the screen is document 2430 on our 65 ter not to be shown to the public, please, and under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, sir, if we look at the last second page in English, and the second page in B/C/S, we'll see, I think it's one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page then in each.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This report deals with a visit of the International Committee of the Red Cross to Manjaca on the 16th of July, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They presented their conclusions to the -- to the commander of the camp, is that right, and to Colonel Vukelic who was the assistant commander for moral guidance of the 1KK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They refer in this report to Omer Filipovic and Senad Supuk being in isolation having been beaten and that there was fresh human blood on the walls of the cell. Had Filipovic and the other gentleman been placed in isolation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Well, since it's written there, I believe it, although I cannot recall it now, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Again in that report you say that military policemen together with the security commander just don't understand that the prisoners are humans. Was that your experience of the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Precisely as I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally the only other paragraph on this report, is the fact that the soldiers, policemen, are sometimes taking, I think it must be out, rather than put, prisoners whom they don't like or who they like less by their own will and that they beat them as they please. Again, sir, was that a fact that unfortunately happened in Manjaca, that there were beatings by the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it is recorded in the report, and I took steps through the military police and I sent the report it itself to my superior, so that certain measures be taken just to put a stop to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And just so we are quite clear, are you referring there just to the military police or to both civilian and military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: This regarded principally the military police because the type of information was normally dealt by a patrol of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be marked -- admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P490 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you just look very briefly, please, at the next document which is -- the number is 2778 on our 65 ter list and need not be under seal. And we need the second page, first of all, in the B/C/S and the second page in English. Sorry, the third page in the B/C/S. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a report of the same incident by Colonel Vukelic dated, in fact, the same day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to go through it again, can we just have that admitted and marked, on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P491, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Moving through quickly, if we can, can we look, next, please, at document 821. Actually, forget that, don't worry, I'm sorry, because of the time it can come in through another witness. Can we look at document 2431. Again, can that be under seal and not put up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Another one of your reports, sir. 22nd of July. And effectively, it's the same theme, isn't it, sir? You say that it should be noted, in the first paragraph, that every new group of prisoners from Kljuc and Sanski Most is less and less incriminated so that you suggest that cases are selected, that this way of bringing prisoners is stopped because if they did not have weapons, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. You are actually making the point that, I think again, that these are not prisoners of war in the proper sense of the word. And you end this paragraph by saying: "Incidentally, this camp can be considered as a detention camp, i.e., a camp for the segregation of Muslims and Croats, which history will not forgive us." You wrote that at the time, sir. Is that still an opinion that you hold?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That is still my opinion, although there is a lot of my own personal input in this report. My own opinions and impressions because that's how I saw it. There were too many people for whom we had no information that they had indeed committed a war crime or that they were captured on front lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then at the beginning of the next paragraph: "During the day, nine new war prisoners were brought into the POW camp Manjaca from Kljuc. Even the militiamen who brought them in did not know how to explain why they had imprisoned them and brought them in. Truth to be said, this is the first group which was brought in tact, i.e., there are no traces of violence, so this is also proof they were probably brought in only because they are Muslims and Croats." Yes, that's what I wanted to ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P492 under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next can we have, please, up on the screen 2432. Again could that be not put up on the screen and marked as under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the following day and you are talking about the 994 prisoners from Sanski Most: "We do not have any new information, i.e., a great number of these prisoners did not take part in combat activities, were not in possession of weapons, and there's no other evidence based on which they could be kept prisoners. We take statements from the prisoners, and these statements come down to two or three sentences, because prisoners don't have anything to say except they were imprisoned whilst at home on that and that date and brought to the camp without knowing the reason for it." And then you appeal once more to the people responsible in the municipalities of Kljuc and Sanski Most not to do this anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, can we look at the last paragraph on page 1 in English. Yes, it's the same in -- page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This deals with an allegation of force by the military police, and you end up by saying: "We warn once again that the military police commander should be informed that the POW camp Manjaca is not a torture house but a camp of war prisoners who should be treated at least humanely."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours, can that be admitted and marked under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P493 under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, can we look, please, at document 365 on our 65 ter list. Sorry, it's already an exhibit, in which case don't worry. I'm sorry, it's already an exhibit. Can we look, please, next -- yes, at document -- sorry, it's 10229. So this one was not on our 65 ter list, Your Honours, and I'll have it marked for identification. And if necessary, apply to have it admitted in a written motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This deals with effectively, is this right, it's one of a number of documents saying that prisoners of war should be engaged as labourers, in this case for the entire length of the water-pipes with the appropriate security. And earlier on you referred to the church being built by the prisoners. Were the prisoners used to do quite a lot of physical labouring work on pipes and other matters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just refer, did you have any difficulty in finding prisoners who wanted to do the work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, the prisoners went out to work on a voluntary basis. It was natural for people to want to be outside in the fresh air and have contact with other people, so the policemen would also like for volunteers to go to work on a particular day, and in addition to the pipeline and digging up potatoes, there was this work on the reconstruction of the church that we'll come to. So it was on voluntary basis, and far more people volunteered than was actually necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Then can we look, please, next very quickly at document 2433 to be under seal, please, and not go up on the screen. The previous one should be MFI'd, sorry, I forgot about that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P494 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if we can have up the document that I've just mentioned, 2433, under seal and not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, sir, another one of your reports. And this report deals with the death of Omer Filipovic and Esad Bender; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so it was a few days after the visit by -- the first visit by -- actually, I didn't ask you that. That visit about which the report was made, was that the first visit of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: I don't think so actually. I can't quite remember when they visited first, but it was quite early on. I think at the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anyhow, I don't think we need -- because of time, so I don't think we've got time to go through this report except to note that the Topic, as you told us, was one of the people suspected of having been a party to the death of these two men? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see that, sorry, I should say, at the top of page 2 in English and it's the second paragraph in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, they were uncovered straightaway, the perpetrators, within the space of half an hour to an hour. And all those who were supposed to be informed about it were, and investigating magistrates team asked for an investigation to be launched. A pathologist was on the scene, and as far as we were concerned, the case was over because it was handed on to other organs and authorities, and the only other thing that I did was to call his brother Mehmed and express my condolences to him on a personal level, talk to him and perhaps we had a cup of coffee.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please admitted and marked, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P495, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you now, please, have a look at 508. 65 ter 508.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a combat, what is called a combat report of the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff and at the bottom of the first page in English and it's the second -- third page in B/C/S. Paragraph 3, we can see that it says: "About 1.460 POWs were brought from Omarska to Manjaca. There were deaths during the transport to the camp." In a moment we'll have a look at your report about that, but was this after the -- the report is dated the 7th of August. Was this after the closure of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, then may that be admitted and marked. It's on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P496, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now could you go, please, to 1587. Sorry, could we have up 1587. And that should be under seal, sorry, and not go on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look at the second page, please, first of all, very quickly, and do we see there in B/C/S as well, please. Is that actually signed by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's dated the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Go back, please, to page 1 in each.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, you are talking about the reception, you say, The lists haven't been updated, certain individuals from the list have been omitted. You don't know if they came from Omarska or not. Eight prisoners died during the transport, three of whom probably have been killed because they had visible traces of violence, and here you talk about: "The behaviour of the people who participated in securing the transportation of prisoners is very incorrect, inhuman, and bullying. When they were warned not to kill a half dead prisoner, they told him 'should you act like that, you'll get what he got?'" Was that person who went and spoke to them about their behaviour, was that you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Yes, because of goings on of this kind in front of the camp, the camp commander intervened as well, but they didn't stop that behaviour, so I went out too. I felt it my duty, moral duty and an -- (redacted) (redacted). I also went out to try to prevent any further willful behaviour, but I came across the scene that you described, and I was told that if I shouted at them, I'll fare the same as the others, so I couldn't do anything else but inform my superior and write this report, as it says here, and I would write the same report today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, can we redact the words at

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: redact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who were the people who brought in these people from Omarska? Not their names, but what was their jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: Of course, I couldn't give you the names because I don't know them, but they were mostly members of the police, the milicija, those were the uniforms they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally on this, in the last paragraph in the English on page 1: "Manjaca camp is now full, has no room for a single prisoner. We are reminding the investigating inspectors explanations that all prisoners who have been brought in from Omarska are serious extremists. He didn't provide a single explanation of that fact. During the reception we have found people who weren't even fit to hold a rifle in their hands, nonetheless to run or to shoot. And we also found minors who didn't even have a weapon or participated in the combat, not being water carriers. All of this is indicative of thoughtless conducts of the organs in Prijedor, the superficial work of the organs of the police and the SUP, and this is the reason why we are requesting you to urgently give us official records ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P497, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I'm trying to cut things out. Yes, could we look now, please, at 2384. Again, Your Honours, please, under seal and not to be on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So is that another one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you describe the composition of the prisoners in the camp and then you talk about in the second paragraph a visit by Vojo Kupresanin who's told apparently arrived and told them that 70 per cent would be released on Thursday, he having visited two days earlier. Who was Mr. Vojo Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-172
